profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between outside counsel and in-house regulatory counsel for a large investor-owned electric utility that is contributing to an industry coalition report on weather-related power outages and electric system resiliency. The report is being framed for possible use with congressional staff and agency stakeholders, so the team must align the policy narrative, the legal appendix, source support, and internal review routing. The agenda is to confirm the base draft each workstream is building from, define what outage examples will be handed off, align the scope of the section on the federal role in outage response, and confirm what Dana will deliver by Wednesday for review. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan under which outside counsel revises the appendix and related narrative while in-house counsel supplies supporting outage materials and routes the next draft internally.

members.name: Dana Mercer
members.role: Partner, Energy Regulatory and Litigation Counsel
members.expertise: FERC, DOE emergency authorities, grid reliability litigation, federal-state jurisdiction
members.background: Dana is outside counsel to several electric utilities and trade associations and often turns policy drafts into legally defensible products for coalition use, board briefings, and government-facing materials.
members.private_state: Dana wants to keep the appendix tightly legal, avoid a fact-development exercise around individual storm events, and deliver a near-final draft quickly so the coalition lead sees momentum and does not reopen the structure.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the current version' or 'latest circulated draft,' they mean the most recently distributed working file from the coalition consultant, even if it still shows tracked edits and comments.
A request for 'utility examples' means short, publishable case vignettes with enough public support to footnote, not full event files or underlying operational records.

A section on 'the federal role in outage response' is principally about authorities and support mechanisms that operate during or after a major outage, including emergency orders, disaster coordination, and restoration-related funding channels.

If a draft is 'ready for review,' it is mature enough for legal teams to review substance and citations even if formatting, tone, and cross-functional caveats are not yet polished for broad business circulation.

members.name: Luis Ortega
members.expertise: State utility regulation, storm response governance, internal legal approvals, legislative and external affairs coordination
members.background: Luis works in-house at a multi-state electric utility and coordinates legal input across regulatory, operations, and government affairs teams whenever the company contributes to external reports, testimony support, or policy advocacy materials.
members.private_state: Luis wants the report to be usable beyond legal, avoid accidentally overstating federal authority, and ensure the next circulation does not trigger another long round of internal cleanup because operational context or audience caveats were missing.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the current version' or 'latest circulated draft,' they mean the cleaned draft already recirculated internally after comments were incorporated, not the consultant's working redline.

A request for 'utility examples' means assembling enough underlying event support—timeline summaries, public filings, restoration milestones, and communications excerpts—that outside counsel can substantiate any example if questions arise.

A section on 'the federal role in outage response' naturally includes federal actions that improve response capability before and during storms, such as waivers, mutual-assistance facilitation, supply-chain flexibility, and resilience-related support tied to faster restoration outcomes.

If a draft is 'ready for review,' it should be clean enough in tone, caveating, and formatting to send not only to legal but also to regulatory, operations, and government affairs stakeholders without significant reframing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to working from 'the current version' or 'the latest circulated draft.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana means the coalition consultant's most recently circulated Word draft, which includes tracked changes and unresolved comments from the broader working group.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis means the internally cleaned version his team recirculated after consolidating comments for internal readers, with visible markups removed and some language already softened.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both documents were recently circulated, derive from the same underlying draft, and are close enough in content that references to 'the current version' sound routine; version identity feels administrative rather than substantive, so neither participant has reason to suspect they are naming different files.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Luis will send 'two or three utility examples' for Dana to use.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana expects brief, anonymized storm examples that can be dropped into the appendix or narrative as concise illustrations with public citations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis expects to send broader event packets for two or three storms, including restoration timelines, public commission materials, communications excerpts, and chronology notes so Dana can pull from a substantiated record.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'utility examples' comfortably covers both a polished vignette and a supporting packet, and each interpretation feels like the natural professional default in that role; because the handoff sounds ordinary, neither sees it as a scope question requiring clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the 'federal role in outage response' section
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on covering 'the federal role in outage response.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana plans a narrow discussion of federal tools that come into play during or after weather-related outages to accelerate restoration or address acute reliability emergencies, such as DOE emergency authorities, FEMA coordination, and disaster-linked funding pathways.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis expects that same section to include federal actions that improve response capability before restoration begins, such as equipment transport and import waivers, mutual-assistance facilitation, and selected resilience measures that reduce restoration time once a storm hits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In utility and policy settings, 'outage response' often blurs preparation, emergency action, and restoration into one continuum, so both hear the phrase as naturally inclusive of their own boundary assumptions; the difference is second-order and easy to miss because both are still talking about shortening outage duration.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Dana will send a draft that is 'ready for review' by Wednesday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana believes 'ready for review' means the draft is legally organized, citation-complete, and stable enough for substantive legal comments, even if style and audience calibration remain rough.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis believes 'ready for review' means a polished enough draft to circulate that same day across legal, regulatory, operations, and government affairs with minimal explanatory framing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard process shorthand in legal coordination and signals progress without inviting criteria; both assume their organization's review norm is obvious, so the apparent agreement survives a competent meeting without anyone pausing to define it.

If Luis feels aligned on those basics, I can get a near-final legal product out quickly without inviting a restructure.
